outcome: No accepted resolution has appeared since 26 January 2024. The only new mathematics in the window is Letzter, Pokrovskiy and Williams (arXiv 2511.11331, Nov 2025), which proves the asymptotic bound gs(T) >= (1-eps)n for large trees and states that the full conjecture remains open. The full-proof preprints by Gnang (2018 onward, 2022) and Mehendale (2005 onward, last revised March 2024) and Gilbert (2007, withdrawn 2010) predate or sit at the edge of the window, are unrefereed, and remain unaccepted and unrefuted in every source I found; Wikipedia, MathWorld and Open Problem Garden all still list the conjecture as open as of Jul-Oct 2026.
problem_asks: Statement: every tree admits a graceful labeling. Parts: (1) the quantifier ranges over all trees, of every finite order n, with no restriction to a class; (2) for each such tree T there exists a graceful labeling, meaning an injective labeling of the vertices by integers 0..m (m = number of edges, under the standard definition, which the bare statement does not spell out) whose induced edge labels |f(u)-f(v)| are pairwise distinct (equivalently exactly {1,...,m}). Equivalent reformulation found in the literature (Letzter et al. 2025): gs(T) = n-1 for every n-vertex tree T, where gs(T) is the maximum number of distinct edge-differences over bijective labelings onto {1,...,n}.

events.what_happened: Dhananjay P. Mehendale, 'On Gracefully Labeling Trees', arXiv math/0503484 (math.GM). Current abstract (v16): 'The main result of this paper is the affirmative settlement of the well-known graceful tree conjecture', via (a) giving label 1 to special vertices and (b) associating distinct lattice paths with trees, with an induction on pendant-vertex deletion; also an algorithm for graceful spanning trees of a clique. The v2 abstract page carries the same sentence 'the graceful tree conjecture is settled in the affirmative in two independent ways' (recursive generation theorem; sequential improvement algorithm). The v1 abstract page, as returned by WebFetch, carries a settlement sentence with different wording ('reconstruction theorem'). The v1 PDF was not readable, so v1 is not confirmed against its body.

events.delivers: Claims a complete proof that every tree is graceful. The abstract states no restriction on the trees covered. The method is claimed to work by labelling special vertices with 1 and by lattice-path induction, but neither method's argument was readable to me.

events.doubts: No refereeing, acceptance, or refutation found. The claim sits in an arXiv math.GM preprint with 16 versions and an unchanged title across all of them. The one recent reference list I read (Letzter, Pokrovskiy and Williams 2025, reference list as summarised by WebFetch) does not cite it, and Wikipedia, MathWorld and Open Problem Garden do not mention it. The 2024 revision's content is unknown to me.
events.direction: Affirmative: claims the conjecture itself (every tree is graceful).

events.what_happened: Edinah K. Gnang, 'On graceful labelings of trees', arXiv 1811.07614 (math.CO). Version history of the abstract: v1 (19 Nov 2018, titled 'On graceful and harmonious labelings of trees') says only that the paper investigates 'an algebraic approach to the Kotzig-Ringel and the Graham-Sloane conjecture' and derives spectra of two families. v2 (26 Nov 2018) says 'We prove the Kotzig-Ringel and the Graham-Sloane conjectures'. v5 (21 Jan 2019) repeats the claim. v12 (1 Jul 2020, current, retitled 'On graceful labelings of trees') says: 'We prove via a composition lemma, the Kotzig-Ringel-Rosa conjecture, better known as the Graceful Labeling Conjecture' and 'We also prove via a stronger version of the composition lemma a stronger form of the Graceful Labeling Conjecture'. The body was not readable to me (abstract pages only).
events.revisions: v1 19 Nov 2018; v2 26 Nov 2018 (first version whose abstract claims a proof); v3 28 Nov 2018; v4 4 Dec 2018; v5 21 Jan 2019; v6 29 Jan 2019; v7 1 Apr 2019; v8 19 May 2019; v9 28 Aug 2019; v10 18 Sep 2019; v11 26 Nov 2019 (retitled 'On graceful, harmonious and poised labelings of trees', per a search snippet); v12 1 Jul 2020 (22 KB). Date given is v1 because the body of v1 is unread; if the judging pass dates the claim by its abstract, use 26 Nov 2018.
events.delivers: Claims a proof of the Kotzig-Ringel-Rosa conjecture, identified with the graceful tree conjecture (every tree admits a graceful labeling), by a composition lemma. The abstract states no restriction on the trees covered. The stronger lemma is said to yield a stronger form of the conjecture, which the abstract does not state.
events.remains: Nothing, if the proof holds. I did not read the body and cannot say whether the composition lemma as stated covers all trees.
events.time_since_posted: About 7.9 years since v2 (Nov 2018). No journal publication, referee report, or expert commentary found in searches.
events.doubts: (a) Gnang's own later note 'On The Composition Lemma' (arXiv 2111.12812, see gnang-2021-composition-lemma) is reported by a search snippet to say that an earlier proof of the composition lemma was 'unnecessarily laborious and incomplete'. I could not read the v1 PDF to verify that wording. (b) The abstract changed within a week from 'investigate an algebraic approach' (v1) to 'We prove' (v2). (c) No independent expert engagement found. (d) The one recent paper I read on the problem (Letzter, Pokrovskiy and Williams 2025) does not cite this work (per its reference list as summarised) and calls the conjecture open.
events.direction: Affirmative: claims the conjecture itself.

events.what_happened: Edinah K. Gnang, 'On The Composition Lemma', arXiv 2111.12812 (math.CO). Abstract, verbatim: 'We describe two distinct simple, short and self contained proofs of the composition lemma.' The lemma is the key input of the 2018 and 2022 claims. A search snippet (not verified; the v1 PDF was unreadable) says the note calls an earlier proof 'unnecessarily laborious and incomplete'.
events.revisions: v1 24 Nov 2021; v2 3 Jan 2022; v3 4 Feb 2022 (current, 15 KB).
events.delivers: Two proofs of the composition lemma as stated in the 2022 paper (Lemma 25, per WebFetch summary): for n > 3 and f with |f^(n-1)(Z_n)| = 1 and G_f of diameter at least 3, the maximum over permutations sigma of the number of distinct values |sigma f^2 sigma^-1(i) - i| is at most the same maximum for f. This is one ingredient of the KRR claim and does not state the conjecture.
events.remains: The KRR/graceful tree statement itself, which depends on this lemma and on the rest of the argument (Theorem 26 and the iteration).
events.doubts: The search snippet (unverified, see above) describes an earlier, incomplete proof of this lemma. The 2022 paper's own proof of the lemma, as summarised by WebFetch, has steps 'asserted rather than fully justified' (its phrases 'It is easy to see that' and 'By construction' are quoted in the summary). That summary is a model's reading of the text, so it needs checking against the paper.
events.direction: Supports the KRR claims in part (a lemma), with no direct settlement of the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Edinah K. Gnang, 'A proof of the Kotzig-Ringel-Rosa Conjecture', arXiv 2202.03178 (math.CO), sole author. v1 abstract, as returned by WebFetch: 'We provide a short and rigorous proof of the Kotzig-Ringel-Rosa conjecture' using 'a functional reformulation of the conjecture and a new composition lemma'. The current abstract (v3) says 'The Kotzig-Ringel-Rosa conjecture asserts that every tree admits a graceful labeling' and that the paper proves it. Per WebFetch's summary of the v3 full text, Theorem 1 states 'Every tree admits a graceful labeling', with Theorem 26 (Graceful Labeling Theorem) proved by iterating the composition lemma until the function is constant; the summary also says the paper claims a first non-asymptotic result on decomposing K_{2n-1} into copies of any n-vertex tree.
events.revisions: v1 4 Feb 2022 (34 KB); v2 14 Aug 2023 (51 KB); v3 31 Jan 2025 (56 KB, current; arXiv admin note 'text overlap with arXiv:2111.12812'). The abstract pages do not say what changed in v2 or v3.
events.delivers: Claims a full proof that every tree admits a graceful labeling (no restriction stated). Route: a functional reformulation (trees as functions on Z_n with a unique attractive fixed point), a graceful-expansion characterisation, a determinantal certificate, and the composition lemma (Lemma 25) which is iterated to reach a constant function; Theorem 1 follows from Theorem 26 as a special case when G_f is connected and f has a fixed point (per WebFetch summary).
events.remains: Nothing, if the proof holds. Whether the composition lemma's proof is complete is the key step; I could not verify it.
events.time_since_posted: About 4.7 years since v1; about 1.7 years since v3 (Jan 2025). No journal publication or referee report found; no expert discussion found in searches.
events.doubts: (a) The composition lemma's proof is summarised as having steps 'asserted rather than fully justified' (quoted phrases in the summary, not verified). (b) Two of the author's own sources (1811.07614, 2111.12812) describe earlier forms of the same lemma; the search snippet for 2111.12812 says the earlier proof was incomplete (unverified). (c) The one recent paper I read (Letzter, Pokrovskiy and Williams 2025) neither cites this work nor reports any gap, and calls the conjecture open. (d) The author still asserts the result in a Dec 2025 talk (gnang-2025-talk). (e) No computer verification is claimed in the text I read.
events.direction: Affirmative: claims a proof of the conjecture for all trees.

events.what_happened: Edinah Gnang (Johns Hopkins University), talk 'A Functional Lens To Graphical Design', Discrete Math Seminar, LGRT 1569, 12 Dec 2025 (UMass event page; the page says the talk has already occurred). The oldest among these conjectures is the Kotzig-Ringel-Rosa conjecture (1964). We will present in our talk a recent simpler and shorter proof of our key lemma and if time permits we will also describe related open problems.'
events.delivers: Restates the claim to settle the KRR conjecture (every tree graceful) by the functional approach, and says a simpler, shorter proof of the key lemma will be presented. The abstract does not name the graceful lemma. I found no written version of the simpler proof dated after 2202.03178 v3 (Jan 2025), so the announced proof may be v3 or may be unwritten.

events.time_since_posted: About 10 months since the talk. The talk restates a claim first made in 2018 and 2022.
events.doubts: The talk announces a 'recent simpler and shorter proof' of a lemma without naming it, and I could not locate that write-up. Restatement is not a new written argument, so by section 5.1 this event does not move the claim's date.
events.direction: Affirmative (restated): claims the KRR conjecture and some other long-standing conjectures.

events.what_happened: Shoham Letzter, Alexey Pokrovskiy and Ella Williams (UCL), 'On the gracesize of trees', arXiv 2511.11331 (math.CO). Defines gs(T) as the maximum number of distinct edge-differences over bijective labellings of an n-vertex tree T onto {1,...,n}, and proves: for every eps > 0 there is n0 such that every tree on n > n0 vertices satisfies gs(T) >= (1-eps)n. The abstract calls the graceful tree conjecture 'longstanding', posed by Rosa in the 1960s. The introduction says research has been fruitful 'yet in full generality it remains open'. Previous bound (Rosa and Siran 1995, per the introduction via summary): gs(T) >= 5(n-1)/7.
events.revisions: v1 14 Nov 2025 (32 KB); v2 31 Jul 2026 (33 KB, current). The v2 change is not stated on the abstract page.
events.delivers: Asymptotic only: every tree with more than n0(eps) vertices has an almost graceful labelling with at least (1-eps)n distinct edge-differences. No exact labelling for any tree is produced, and small trees are not covered.
events.remains: The exact conjecture: every tree (of every order) has gs(T) = n-1, i.e. is graceful. Also the small-tree range, which the bound does not reach.
events.time_since_posted: About 11 months since v1; about 2.5 months since v2 (31 Jul 2026). No journal version found, and no commentary found in searches.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture asymptotically; does not prove it for any tree.

events.what_happened: Edinah K. Gnang and Isaac Wass, 'Growing Graceful and Harmonious Trees', arXiv 1808.05551 (math.CO). Abstract (as split by WebFetch): symbolic constructions for listing and enumerating graphs with the same induced edge-label sequence; 'We settle in the affirmative R. Whitty's [W08] conjectured existence of determinantal constructions for listing and enumerating gracefully labeled trees'; and a new graceful labelling algorithm.
events.delivers: Settles a different conjecture (Whitty's, on determinantal constructions for listing and enumerating gracefully labelled trees). It does not assert that every tree is graceful.
events.remains: The graceful tree conjecture, which the abstract does not address.
events.direction: Neutral to the conjecture: a result on a different question (enumeration and constructions), discounted here.

events.what_happened: Matt Superdock, 'New graceful diameter-6 trees by transfers', arXiv 1402.6570 (math.CO). Shows that certain trees with a designated central vertex admit graceful labellings with the root labelled 0, under conditions including: complete diameter-6 trees, diameter-2r complete trees, and diameter-6 trees where every internal vertex has an odd number of children (the abstract highlights that all depth-3 trees with odd-children internal vertices are graceful).
events.delivers: Restricted classes only: certain diameter-6 trees, complete diameter-2r trees, and trees with odd-children conditions. It does not settle the conjecture for any class covering all trees.
events.remains: All trees outside these classes, which is nearly all trees.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture on restricted classes; does not move the general statement.

events.what_happened: Jocelyn R. Bell, Lotenna Nwobbi, Connor Parrow, Alexandria Wheeler and Ephrata Zelleke, 'Graceful wind chimes', Involve, a Journal of Mathematics 14(4), pp. 683-696, published 23 Oct 2021. Abstract: 'It has been an open question for more than 50 years whether or not every tree has a graceful labeling.' It introduces 'wind chimes' (a class of trees) and proves that wind chimes meeting certain criteria are graceful.
events.delivers: A restricted class (wind chimes meeting stated criteria). Does not settle the conjecture.
events.remains: All trees outside the wind-chime class; the abstract says the question is also unknown for trees of maximum degree 3.
events.time_since_posted: About 5 years (journal publication, Oct 2021). I did not check whether an earlier preprint exists, so the first public version may be earlier.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture on a restricted class; does not move the general statement.

events.what_happened: Anna Adamaszek, Peter Allen, Codrut Grosu and Jan Hladky, 'Almost all trees are almost graceful', arXiv 1608.01577 (Aug 2016); Random Structures and Algorithms 56(4), 2020, pp. 948-987. Proves that for large n, trees of maximum degree O(n/log n) admit labelings with labels from {1,...,(1+c)n} for any c > 0, so almost all trees on n vertices admit a relaxed labelling; the proof uses a natural randomised algorithm. Gives an approximate version of the Ringel-Kotzig conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 4 Aug 2016; v2 8 Aug 2016; v3 14 Nov 2017; v4 3 Dec 2018; v5 25 May 2019; v6 24 Sep 2019 (current). Journal: Random Structures and Algorithms 56(4), 2020 (per the arXiv journal reference).
events.delivers: A relaxed version only: labels up to (1+c)n rather than n-1, for bounded-degree trees and almost all trees. Does not give a graceful labelling for any particular tree.
events.remains: The exact conjecture for every tree; and even the relaxed statement for every tree, since it is proved only for almost all.

Weisstein, reports that a proposed inductive route (each graceful rooted tree admits a graceful one-leaf extension at its root, which would prove the conjecture by induction) holds 'for all 97,055,181 types of rooted trees on 22 vertices'. The entry says this is not yet an inductive proof.

events.what_happened: Blog post 'Graceful Graph Moves' by the author of prideout.net (Philip Rideout, who wrote the blog's 2020 post on this conjecture; the 2026 post says it was written for Arcol). Undated in the text; the draft file names carry 30 May and 1 June 2026. It gives constructive proofs, by graph transformations that preserve graceful labellings, that paths and caterpillars are graceful, plus double stars; it attributes banana trees to Sethuraman and Jesintha (2009) and cites the diameter-5 case (Hrnčiar and Haviar) as out of scope. It says that if the conjecture is true it implies Ringel's tree-packing conjecture, and that spiders and lobsters have 'not been settled', although 'various subfamilies have been proven to be graceful'. It says 'GPT-5.5 taught me about different families of trees that have been proven to be graceful' and describes many conversations with GPT-5.5 about the conjecture.
events.revisions: Two draft file stamps: 20260530 and 20260601 (names only; the text gives no date).
events.delivers: Re-proofs of families already known in the literature (paths, caterpillars, double stars, and cited banana-tree and diameter-5 results). Nothing new for the general statement, and the post does not describe any proof as new.
events.remains: Spiders, lobsters, and every tree outside the families above; the general statement.
events.directly_checkable: The constructions for paths and caterpillars are elementary and can be checked by hand from the post's transfer moves.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture on known families; no move on the general statement.

events.what_happened: Blog post 'Graceful Lean' (prideout.net/blog/graceful-lean/), undated (it follows 'Graceful Graph Moves'). It formalises graph predicates and two statements in Lean, path_graph_is_graceful and caterpillar_graph_is_graceful, and gives proofs built on recipe types. The proofs depend on three axioms not proved in Lean (path_graph_has_recipe, caterpillar_graph_has_recipe, extreme_sprout_theorem). The post says the initial statements had sorry placeholders which the later proofs replace, and that it was written 'primarily to teach myself' Lean.
events.delivers: Formal statements and partial proofs for paths and caterpillars only, depending on three unproved axioms. Discounted: known families, not the general statement.
events.remains: All other trees, and the general conjecture.

disputes.summary: Proof claims versus status: Mehendale (2005, 'settled in the affirmative'), Gnang (2018 v2 'We prove', 2022 'a short and rigorous proof', and the Dec 2025 talk) and Gilbert (2007, withdrawn 2010) claim full proofs. Wikipedia (last edited 21 Jul 2026), MathWorld (last updated 2 Oct 2026), Open Problem Garden, Letzter, Pokrovskiy and Williams (Nov 2025, v2 Jul 2026) and Bell et al. (2021) describe the conjecture as open. None of the sources I read accepts or refutes any of the claims, and the author-side claims have no referee record.

Krishnaa (2004): a Ukrainian review by Petrenyuk (2016, search snippet only; full text not opened) says Krishnaa's 2004 proof and Gilbert's 2009 proof were 'wrong or incomplete'. Krishnaa's Informatica 2004 paper (abstract snippet only) is a survey whose abstract says the Ringel-Kotzig conjecture remained unsolved and does not present a proof. The claim that Krishnaa proposed a proof therefore rests only on the secondary review, and I could not verify it.
Horton's extension: MathWorld lists 28 vertices (Horton 2003); Wikipedia says 29 (Michael Horton honours thesis). Unresolved; the thesis was not opened.

summary:
Searches found no accepted resolution of the graceful tree conjecture, and no source that accepts or refutes the full-proof preprints. The live claims are Mehendale (arXiv math/0503484, 2005; v16 revised Mar 2024), Gilbert (arXiv 0709.2201, 2007; withdrawn 2010) and Gnang (arXiv 1811.07614, claim from v2 of Nov 2018; arXiv 2202.03178, Feb 2022, v3 Jan 2025), with Gnang's composition-lemma note (2111.12812, 2021) and a Dec 2025 talk restating the claim. None of these has a journal record or a referee report I could find. The only recent mathematics bearing on the conjecture is Letzter, Pokrovskiy and Williams (arXiv 2511.11331, Nov 2025; v2 Jul 2026), which proves the asymptotic bound gs(T) >= (1-eps)n for large trees and states that the conjecture 'in full generality remains open'. The paper's visible reference list does not include Gnang, Mehendale or Gilbert (per a WebFetch summary, not a character check). Wikipedia (edited 21 Jul 2026), MathWorld (updated 2 Oct 2026) and Open Problem Garden all call the conjecture open. Computational verification stands at 35 vertices (Fang 2010, arXiv 1003.3045), with unpublished claims to 39 (Fang 2012, per MathWorld) and a MathWorld report from 20 Aug 2026 that a proposed inductive route holds for all 97,055,181 rooted trees on 22 vertices, which MathWorld says is not yet a proof. Restricted-class results include Superdock (2014), Bell et al. (2021, wind chimes), and Adamaszek et al. (2016, a relaxed almost-all-trees result).

The call that matters most is whether Gnang's composition-lemma argument counts as a proof. The 2018 and 2022 abstracts claim one, and the 2025 talk restates it, but I could only read abstracts and WebFetch summaries of the full text. The summary of the 2022 text reports several steps 'asserted rather than fully justified', and the 2021 search snippet says an earlier version of the lemma's proof was 'unnecessarily laborious and incomplete'. Both are unverified. Gilbert's withdrawal and Samal's 2009 comment are a weak signal against his claim only. Mehendale's v16 (Mar 2024, 18 KB, after 306 KB at v15) is a revision inside the window that I could not inspect.

AI involvement: no source I read credits an AI system with any part of the mathematics on this conjecture. The Gnang papers, Letzter et al., Mehendale, Gilbert, Fang and the restricted-class papers name no AI system in the text I read. The one AI-named source on the conjecture itself is Rideout's 2026 blog post 'Graceful Graph Moves', which describes many conversations with GPT-5.5 and says it 'taught me about different families of trees that have been proven to be graceful'. The post attributes no proof to the model and presents its proofs as the author's, so I record none_found false with an empty systems list, as an involvement that stops at teaching and literature. A separate 2026 preprint (Kulkarni, Chakraborty and Bagga, arXiv 2602.05059) credits ChatGPT 5.1 with a proof of a solved line-graph graceful question, but that is a different question and I discount it. Searches for AlphaEvolve, FunSearch, AlphaProof, Aristotle, Gemini and OpenAI for Science found nothing on this conjecture. Knuth's Claude's Cycles note (Feb-Mar 2026) concerns a different problem. The Quanta article on AI in mathematics (Aug 2026) does not mention graceful labellings.

One unverified attribution to note: MathWorld cites Knuth (TAOCP vol. 4 fascicle 7, 2025, p. 24) for the remark that the conjecture is 'almost certainly true'. I could not read Knuth's PDF (returned as binary), so the remark is attributed by MathWorld only. It is a view, not an event.
competing_reading: The 2018 and 2022 Gnang preprints (and possibly Mehendale's 2005 preprint) are correct, and the conjecture was settled before the window. On this reading the Wikipedia, MathWorld, and Open Problem Garden entries are out of date, and the 2025 Letzter et al. paper is a partial result written without knowledge of the earlier claim. The author's own repair of the composition lemma in 2021 and the Dec 2025 talk's 'simpler and shorter proof' would then be the author's answers to any gap, and the Lean project would be an independent machine check. Under this reading the window contains no new settlement, and the status question was decided at the claim's first version, in 2018 or 2022, with no expert record either way.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A referee report, journal acceptance, or published expert verification of arXiv 2202.03178 or 1811.07614, especially of the composition lemma and Theorem 26 of 2202.03178. (2) The Lean 4 project from the 'Towards a formal Lean4 proof that all trees are graceful' talk: its repository, its date, whether it is sorry-free and axiom-free for the general theorem, and what it formalises. (3) A statement from Wikipedia, MathWorld, Open Problem Garden, or Letzter, Pokrovskiy and Williams that addresses the Gnang claims, or a later paper that cites them. (4) Readable copies of the v1 PDFs of Mehendale (2005) and Gnang (2021, 2111.12812) to check the first-version claim and the 'incomplete' wording. (5) The text of Mehendale's v16 (Mar 2024) to see what the 2024 revision changed. (6) The Horton thesis, to settle 28 vs 29 vertices.

event.what_happened: Shoham Letzter, Alexey Pokrovskiy and Ella Williams (UCL), 'On the gracesize of trees', arXiv 2511.11331 (math.CO). Defines gs(T) as the maximum number of distinct edge-differences over bijective labellings of an n-vertex tree T onto {1,...,n}, and proves: for every eps > 0 there is n0 such that every tree on n > n0 vertices satisfies gs(T) >= (1-eps)n. The abstract calls the graceful tree conjecture 'longstanding', posed by Rosa in the 1960s. The introduction says research has been fruitful 'yet in full generality it remains open'. Previous bound (Rosa and Siran 1995, per the introduction via summary): gs(T) >= 5(n-1)/7.
event.revisions: v1 14 Nov 2025 (32 KB); v2 31 Jul 2026 (33 KB, current). The v2 change is not stated on the abstract page.
event.delivers: Asymptotic only: every tree with more than n0(eps) vertices has an almost graceful labelling with at least (1-eps)n distinct edge-differences. No exact labelling for any tree is produced, and small trees are not covered.
event.remains: The exact conjecture: every tree (of every order) has gs(T) = n-1, i.e. is graceful. Also the small-tree range, which the bound does not reach.
event.time_since_posted: About 11 months since v1; about 2.5 months since v2 (31 Jul 2026). No journal version found, and no commentary found in searches.
event.direction: Supports the conjecture asymptotically; does not prove it for any tree.

judgement.why: The only post-snapshot mathematics on the statement itself is Letzter-Pokrovskiy-Williams, an asymptotic gracesize bound: bound, unreviewed, credible. Full-proof claims all predate the snapshot: Mehendale's 2005 claim keeps its 2005 date since the March 2024 v16 shows no identified new mathematics (F1), and it is set aside as not_credible given two decades of silence, math.GM, endless revisions and later work calling the problem open; Gilbert is withdrawn; Gnang 2018/2022 are kept as doubtful (established author, serious method, but a self-acknowledged incomplete lemma proof and no uptake) and are whole/unreviewed, so they tier only as pre-snapshot claims. The Gnang talk restates without new written argument (none). Rideout's posts re-prove known families (none); GPT-5.5 only taught literature, so none. Finite verifications are instances. Kulkarni et al. concerns line graphs, a variant; its ChatGPT 5.1 proof is recorded as generated for that event only, and the variant scope discards it. Adamaszek et al. proves a relaxed labelling, treated as variant rather than bound.
judgement.doubts: Mehendale v16 (Mar 2024, 'fully revised', 306 KB to 18 KB) was not read; if it contained a genuinely new argument it would be a post-snapshot claim, though it would still be not_credible on the same signals. Adamaszek et al. could arguably be a bound on an approximate quantity rather than a variant; it is pre-snapshot either way. The Kulkarni verification rests on one unnamed faculty expert, and Clark et al.'s 'digested' rests on journal publication reported by snippet.
